channel.title: Building NODE
channel.description: Sven on the questions he runs into while building NODE Research Browser, and what he decides.

item.title: What happens to tabs that aren't on the canvas?
item.description: Options: They fly into their row in the sidebar timeline (dropped); They fade out (chosen). Decided: When you reach the canvas, tabs that aren't cards fade out where they are, and they fade back in when you come down to the Gallery. Why: The canvas only shows pages you've spent time on. A tab you just opened isn't a card yet, and it's still in the timeline.

item.title: What happens when you pinch from a page out to the canvas?
item.description: Options: Swap one view for the next (dropped); Each page travels to its place in the next view (chosen). Decided: Each page is one object. Pinch out and it shrinks into its Mosaic tile, then its Gallery thumbnail, then flies to its card on the canvas. Going up takes 320 ms and coming back takes 200 ms. Labels and lines show up after the pages land. Why: It's the same page at every level, so it should look like it. Next: In NODE pages are native views, so the Gallery and canvas steps will move still pictures of each page, then swap the live page back in.

item.title: Where else should NODE move?
item.description: Plan: I went through every spec and listed the places that still cut from one state to the next. The trail canvas and sharing had almost no motion. First five: the zoom ladder, a page becoming a card, Replay, the highlight in the command bar, and a flash of light when you take a screenshot. Why: The first three show how a trail grows, which is the main idea in NODE. The last two are small and used all the time. Next: A page becoming a card.

item.title: How should NODE show it's reading the page and finding suggestions?
item.description: Options: The page loader's line doing both jobs (dropped); A readout of how NODE scores each word (dropped); Light that splits into keywords (chosen). Decided: A line fills while NODE reads the page. It splits into a thin drop of light for each keyword, each a faint colour of the spectrum, and the keyword lands at the foot of its drop. Each result card draws its left edge in light, then fades in. With the suggestions panel closed and the sidebar hidden, it runs on the right edge of the window, where the panel opens: a tick for each keyword, then a dash for each result that stays in grey as a count. With the sidebar showing, it runs inside the Suggest button. Why: Reading a page takes a few seconds, and until now you couldn't see it happen.

item.title: Should the page loader look like glass?
item.description: Options: A glass lens that slides across the address bar (dropped); Light as a wave, then as particles once data arrives (dropped); White light split into a spectrum (dropped); Light twisted into colour by sugar water (dropped); One line with light and a little refraction at its tip (chosen). Decided: One 2 px line. Nothing shows for the first 200 ms, so fast pages never flash a loader. While the site hasn't answered, a short segment crosses every 1.2 s. Then the line fills with progress, flashes once and fades. If the page fails, it fills red. Its light builds toward the tip and falls softly onto the page. At the tip the light splits into a faint spectrum: red a pixel behind, blue a pixel ahead. I kept the glow small and the colour subtle. Why: I wanted refraction, and trying the bigger ideas showed me a loader on every page has to stay quiet. Next: The glow and the extra colour break NODE's own brand guide, so I need to decide whether the loader gets an exception.

item.title: Where can a loader go when pages sit on top of NODE?
item.description: Options: A thin layer on the edge of the window (chosen); A bar across the top of the page (dropped); Only in the sidebar (dropped). Decided: The loader runs on the left edge of the window, in its own thin layer, the same way the full-screen toolbar does. When the sidebar is open, it sits on the sidebar's edge. Why: With the sidebar hidden, the page fills the window, and the edge is the only place left.

item.title: Can NODE send one count after your first session?
item.description: Options: One anonymous count after your first session (chosen); Only count people who opt in (dropped); No A/B tests, only usability tests (dropped). Decided: Yes. After your first session, NODE sends one anonymous count: which test version you're in, and yes or no for reaching 3 cards, opening the canvas, and sending a trail or pairing a device. There's no id, and nothing about what you read or search. The same switch in Settings → Help turns it off. Why: Without it I'd be running tests I can't read. It's more than NODE sends today, so it'll be said plainly on the welcome screen, in the privacy page and in the release notes before it ships. Next: It ships with the first test, in 0.13. The site's privacy section changes in that release, not before.

item.title: How do I know if people come back, without tracking them?
item.description: Options: Add a "days since install" bucket to the anonymous daily count (chosen); Keep first-week milestones on your computer, with an opt-in to share a summary (also doing); Usability tests with 5 people (also doing); An install id (dropped). Decided: The daily count gets a "days since install" bucket and the test version. First-week milestones stay on your computer unless you choose to share a summary. Why: The daily count has no id, so it can't tell a new user from an old one. Picking the moment that makes people stay without any data to check it would be a guess. Next: Both are on the backlog for 0.13, after their screens are designed.

item.title: How do I test these changes?
item.description: Options: A/B test the three biggest changes at the same time, on new installs (chosen); A/B test them one at a time (dropped); Usability tests with 5 people (also doing); Ship to everyone and compare before and after (dropped); Only count people who opt in (dropped). Decided: I'll A/B test the first screen, the first-card note and the Continue page all at once, on new installs from 0.13. Each new install gets its own coin flip for each change, so every test still compares half of new installs with the other half. Each test only looks for a big difference, because NODE doesn't have the traffic to see small ones yet. I'll set the sample size before each test starts, decide once it's reached, and post the result here, win or not. Why: These are my biggest guesses about the first week, and I'd rather know than assume. Existing users won't be in any test, and Settings will say which version you're in, with a switch to leave. Next: Nothing gets built until I've designed the screens for it and I'm happy with them. All three ship together in 0.13. The count these tests need is decided in "Can NODE send one count after your first session?"

item.title: What brings people back after the first day?
item.description: Options: A Continue page on every new tab, with your open questions and the next search (leaning); System notifications, including one if you skip a day you usually use NODE (later); A weekly email (dropped); Nothing, and rely on tabs reopening (dropped). Plan: A Continue page that replaces the blank new tab. It shows your open trails, each with its open question and the next suggested search. Why: An open question is the best reason to come back, and the new tab is the moment you can act on it. Notifications that do the job forever, without that reason, wear thin. Next: Aiming for 0.13, as an A/B test against a blank new tab, running alongside the other two tests.

item.title: How should you notice your first card?
item.description: Options: A short note and one pulse on the Canvas tab (leaning); Stay silent and let people find the canvas (dropped); A "3 cards to your first trail" checklist (later). Plan: After about 20 seconds of reading, a short note says "First card on your trail" and the Canvas tab pulses once. At 3 cards, one notice offers to show the trail. Why: Today a page becomes a card with no sign at all. Next: Part of the 0.13 first run, as an A/B test against staying silent.

item.title: What should the first five minutes of NODE feel like?
item.description: Options: A start screen that asks "What are you looking into?" (leaning); Open a finished example trail first (also offered); No start screen, just a helpful empty first tab (fallback); Keep the setup form, cut to one screen with Skip (dropped). Plan: I want first launch to ask "What are you looking into?" instead of asking for API keys. Every way in should end with a trail of 3 cards, the canvas open, and an offer to send it. Why: Right now the first screen is a setup form. The trail, the part that makes NODE different, shows up later on a screen I never point anyone to. Next: I'm aiming to build it for 0.13 and A/B test it against the empty first tab, alongside a 5-person usability test.

item.title: How far do I go to make NODE a habit?
item.description: Plan: No feed, no streaks and no fake urgency. Every kind of notice gets its own switch, and first-week milestones are counted only on your computer. If a change brings more visits but also more people turning notices off, I roll it back. Why: A lot of you picked NODE for privacy. And the long experiments I read, at Facebook and Pinterest, found that pushing harder loses people over a few months.

item.title: Should syncing between devices need an account?
item.description: Options: Pair devices with a code or a QR code (chosen); Sign in with an account (dropped). Decided: No. You pair devices with a code or a QR code, and your trails are encrypted on your device before they're sent. The server deletes each change once your other devices have it, after 30 days at most. This shipped in 0.12.0. Why: A pairing code is enough to prove two devices belong together.

item.title: Should NODE count how many people use it?
item.description: Decided: Yes, with one anonymous count a day: the version and your operating system, with no id. You can turn it off in Settings → Help. This shipped in 0.11.0. Why: Download numbers didn't tell me whether anyone kept using NODE. Nothing about what you read or search is sent.

item.title: How many notifications should NODE send?
item.description: Options: Send more to bring people back (dropped); A weekly limit, only for something new, with a switch per kind (chosen); Ask for permission at first launch (dropped). Decided: Few, and only about something new. There's a weekly limit across all kinds, a switch for each kind, and I'll only ask for system permission on day 3 or later. I judge them by how many people turn them off, not by clicks. Why: The long experiments I read found that fewer, more relevant notifications raise use over time.

item.title: Who is NODE for?
item.description: Options: A browser for one person doing niche research (dropped); Knowledge networking between friends and small groups (chosen). Decided: Knowledge networking between friends and small groups. You map what you read, and send the whole trail to a friend or a group as one file. Why: Research usually gets passed on as a list of links, and the next person starts over. NODE already records the path, so sending it takes no copying.

item.title: What should NODE be called?
item.description: Options: Scout (dropped); NODE R-X Browser (dropped); Node Browser (dropped); NODE Research Browser (chosen). Decided: NODE Research Browser. Why: "Research Browser" says what it is.

item.title: Do I share trails as links or as files?
item.description: Options: One plain Markdown file (chosen); A share link (later). Decided: As one plain Markdown file first. Links come once the share server works for everyone. Why: A file works today, anyone can read it in a text editor, and it outlives the app.

item.title: Should two people's trails merge into one?
item.description: Options: Merge two trails into one (parked); One person builds a trail and shares it (chosen); Show both trails on one canvas, then add chosen cards, then full merge (later). For now: Not yet. I'm focusing on one person building a trail and sharing it. Why: Git-style merging makes sense to developers, but most people researching together don't think that way.

item.title: Is a trail a timeline or a map?
item.description: Options: A timeline only (dropped); A map only (dropped); A canvas with the timeline beside it, and Replay (chosen). Decided: A canvas, with the timeline kept beside it and Replay for whoever receives it. NODE draws the links it already knows. Drawing your own is optional. Why: In the studies I read, people rarely draw links by hand, so NODE draws the ones it knows.

item.title: Can NODE run Chrome extensions?
item.description: Options: Ship uBlock Origin itself (dropped); Ship uBlock Origin Lite (not possible); Support the Chrome Web Store (dropped); Use uBlock Origin's default filter lists in NODE's own blocker (chosen); A Chromium build, which runs extensions (later). Decided: No. Instead, NODE's built-in blocker uses the same filter lists uBlock Origin uses by default. Why: A beta tester asked for uBlock Origin, and this covers what they used it for without breaking NODE's own blocker.

item.title: Electron or a Chromium build?
item.description: Options: Ship NODE as a Chrome extension (dropped); Keep Electron for releases and build on Chromium alongside (chosen); Build on BrowserOS (dropped). So far: Electron stays the release build. I've started a Chromium build on ungoogled-chromium, mainly so Google sign-in works inside NODE. Why: Google blocks sign-in inside Electron apps, and faking Chrome breaks Google's terms. Mosaic and the address-bar suggestions need changes to Chromium itself, so I'll only switch once it does everything the current build does.
